summary: Defines an architecture for providing scalable service differentiation in the Internet. It describes how traffic is classified and marked at the edges and given different treatment in the middle of the network. It is informational and updated by RFC 3260.

plainLanguage.summary: On a highway, some lanes are for fast cars and others for slow trucks. This is the plan for giving different kinds of internet traffic different lanes.

questions: what is the differentiated services architecture
how does diffserv provide quality of service
subtitle: Scalable service differentiation: mark packets at the edge, give them different treatment hop by hop.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs different levels of service for different traffic, without keeping per-flow or per-customer state in the core of the network.
tldr.mechanism: Packets are classified and marked with a DS codepoint at network boundaries, then each node applies a per-hop behavior to the aggregate of packets sharing a codepoint.
tldr.outcome: Complex work stays at the edges and the core stays simple. The RFC is Informational and is updated by RFC 3260.

facts.label: Where marking is carried
facts.value: DS field in the IPv4 or IPv6 header

today: RFC 2475 is an Informational document and is updated by RFC 3260. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata, and it relies on the DS field defined in RFC 2474.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 2475 defines an architecture for differentiated services (often called DiffServ). A service here means characteristics of packet transmission in one direction across a set of paths, such as throughput, delay, jitter, loss or relative priority. The goals are to meet different application needs and to permit differentiated pricing of Internet service.

Scalability comes from two ideas. Complex classification and conditioning happen only at network boundary nodes, and the core applies per-hop behaviors to aggregates of traffic marked in the DS field of the IPv4 or IPv6 header (defined in RFC 2474). No per-application-flow or per-customer state is needed in the core. The architecture is asymmetric: it differentiates service in one direction only.

The requirements list includes working with existing applications without host changes, not depending on hop-by-hop signaling, using only a small set of forwarding behaviors, and allowing incremental deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every road worker remembering every single car, only the toll booths at the entrance check cars and stick a colored label on them. Inside, workers just look at the label.

sections.title: Domains, Boundaries and the Core
sections.content:
A DS domain is a contiguous set of DS nodes that share a service provisioning policy and a set of PHB groups. It normally sits under one administration, such as an organization's intranet or an ISP. Its edge consists of DS boundary nodes, which classify and possibly condition incoming traffic; everything else is a DS interior node. A boundary node acts as an ingress node for traffic entering and an egress node for traffic leaving.

A DS region is a set of contiguous DS domains. To offer services across domains, neighbors set up a peering Service Level Agreement (SLA), from which a Traffic Conditioning Agreement (TCA) says how traffic is conditioned at the boundary. A host can itself act as a boundary node for its own traffic.

The RFC contrasts DiffServ with other models: relative priority marking such as IPv4 Precedence, service marking such as IPv4 TOS, label switching such as Frame Relay, ATM and MPLS, Integrated Services with RSVP, and static per-hop classification. Each either needs more state in the core, more management, or fits fewer future services.
sections.plainLanguage: A network run by one company is like a theme park with gates. The gate staff check tickets and stamp hands. Inside, ride staff only look at the stamp.

sections.title: Classifying and Conditioning Traffic
sections.content:
At a boundary, a classifier selects packets. A BA classifier looks only at the DS codepoint. A multi-field (MF) classifier looks at a combination of fields such as source and destination address, DS field, protocol ID, ports and incoming interface. Selected packets are steered to a traffic conditioner, which may contain four elements.

A traffic profile (for example a token bucket with rate r and burst size b) decides whether a packet is in-profile or out-of-profile. Out-of-profile packets may be queued until they conform (shaped), discarded (policed), given a new codepoint (re-marked), or forwarded while triggering accounting. A dropper can be seen as a shaper with a buffer of zero or a few packets.

Conditioners can sit in the source domain, where packets are pre-marked and classification is simpler, at the boundary of a DS domain, or inside the domain. A DS ingress node must assume that incoming traffic may not conform to the TCA and be ready to enforce it.
sections.plainLanguage: At the gate, a guard looks at who you are, times how fast you are walking in, stamps you, and may slow you down or turn you away if you break the rules.

sections.title: Per-Hop Behaviors
sections.content:
A per-hop behavior (PHB) is the externally observable forwarding behavior a DS node applies to a behavior aggregate, that is, to all packets with the same DS codepoint crossing a link in one direction. The simplest example guarantees a minimum share of a link to an aggregate. PHBs describe behavior, not implementation: nodes realize them with buffer management and packet scheduling, and many mechanisms may fit one PHB.

Related PHBs are specified together as a PHB group. Every codepoint must map to some PHB, and codepoints with no standardized mapping should map to the Default PHB. Section 3 gives guidelines G.1 to G.15 for writing a PHB specification. Examples: it must specify a recommended codepoint, it should state how it behaves under tunneling, it should include conformance requirements and security implications, and a PHB for local use should not be standardized.

The DS field is not used as an input to route selection, and the RFC leaves the control of resource allocation inside a domain largely out of scope, noting that the most scalable model runs nodes open-loop with only administrative-timescale management.
sections.plainLanguage: A per-hop behavior is the rule each worker follows for a labeled package, like 'blue labels go to the front of the line.' The rule says what happens, not which machine does it.

sections.title: Non-DS Nodes and Multicast
sections.content:
A legacy node implements IPv4 Precedence as in RFC 791 and RFC 1812 but is not otherwise DS-compliant. Precedence values are intentionally compatible with the Class Selector Codepoints of RFC 2474, so a domain that uses only those codepoints can tolerate legacy nodes. Other non-DS-compliant nodes may behave unpredictably for non-zero codepoints. The RFC assumes the TOS markings of RFC 1349 are deprecated.

When traffic crosses into a non-DS-capable domain, an egress node may follow an agreement, re-mark to Class Selector Codepoints if it knows the next domain is legacy, or re-mark to zero if it knows nothing, assuming best-effort treatment.

Multicast raises two issues. Replicated packets use more network resources than unicast, and group membership can be dynamic, so quantitative guarantees are hard. Also, a multicast packet may leave through several egress nodes toward different domains, so its codepoint must not violate any peering SLA. One suggested remedy is a separate peering SLA and separate codepoints for multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: If your package goes through a town that does not understand the colored labels, you either use labels the old workers know or take the label off and treat it like normal mail.

sections.title: Security and Tunneling
sections.content:
Because the DS field selects better or worse service, an adversary may steal service by changing it or injecting packets with a valuable codepoint, which can become a denial of service. The main defense is that ingress nodes must condition all traffic entering a domain. Packets with unacceptable codepoints must be discarded or modified, for example reset to the Default PHB codepoint. Interior nodes are not required to check codepoints but must not crash on unacceptable ones. A link that cannot be adequately secured should be treated as a boundary link.

IPsec does not include the DS field in its cryptographic calculations, so it neither breaks when the field changes nor protects it. Tunnel mode protects the inner header's DS field, and the current IPsec requirement is that decapsulation must not change it. A tunnel egress node must act as a DS ingress node unless a sufficiently strong integrity check lets it trust the inner field.

Failed checks are auditable events. Where DS support is added to a system with auditing, administrators must be able to turn DS auditing on or off, and no message is to be sent back to the purported sender, to avoid inducing denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: If a cheater paints a fast-lane stamp on their own hand, the guards at the gate must notice and wipe it off. Tunnels are sealed envelopes: the stamp inside cannot be changed on the way.

items.title: Classifier
items.text: Selects packets by the DS codepoint (BA) or several header fields (MF).

items.title: Meter
items.text: Measures the stream against a traffic profile.

items.title: Marker
items.text: Sets the DS codepoint, possibly re-marking the packet.

items.title: Shaper
items.text: Delays packets to fit the traffic profile.

items.title: Dropper
items.text: Discards packets to fit the profile; this is policing.
